item.title: Criminals run amok in Dhaka, shootings and killings over trivial incidents
item.description:
A series of shootings, killings, robberies and other violent crimes in Dhaka in recent days has raised fresh concerns over the deteriorating law and order situation, with criminals increasingly resorting to violence over seemingly trivial incidents.
In the latest incident, a 27-year-old expatriate youth was stabbed to death after a group of local criminals allegedly entered a house in the capital’s Adarshapara area of Sabujbagh yesterday afternoon.
The victim, Sifat Ullah, was visiting his girlfriend when the group allegedly tried to drag him downstairs. A scuffle followed, during which the attackers hacked him indiscriminately, leaving him critically injured. He later died at a hospital.
Two others were also injured in the incident.
The killing came amid a string of violent incidents across the capital, including a businessman being shot inside his shop in Shani Akhra, a woman being shot at her home in Darus Salam and the recovery of an unidentified man’s body from the Airport-bound elevated expressway in Banani.
In another incident, a man carrying Tk38 lakh after withdrawing the money from a bank was robbed by a group of motorcycle-borne criminals in Dhanmondi.
According to locals, Sifat was at the house of his girlfriend, Nazifa Sheikh, when six or seven local criminals, including Joy, Rajib and Yasin, entered the premises and tried to take him downstairs.
Nazifa said Sifat resisted and a scuffle broke out. The attackers then stabbed him repeatedly, while Rajib and Yasin were also injured.
Sifat was taken to a hospital, where he died later that evening.
Nazifa said she had been in a relationship with Sifat for around two years and that their families were discussing their marriage.
She identified Joy as a known criminal in the area.
However, Rajib alias Rabbi gave a different account, claiming that they had gone to the house after receiving information that immoral activities were taking place there. He alleged that Sifat attacked them with a sharp weapon, triggering the confrontation.
In Shani Akhra, businessman Aslam Khan, 40, was shot inside his Lucky Crockeries shop in front of Royal Hospital.
He suffered gunshot wounds to his left elbow and the right side of his face and was taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
Aslam’s friend Anwar Hossain said two men entered the shop and one of them shot Aslam.
Locals managed to detain one suspect, while another fled the scene.
Anwar called for stronger security measures, saying businesspeople were increasingly concerned about their safety.
In Darus Salam, the Rapid Action Battalion arrested three people, including the husband of a woman who was shot at her home.
RAB-4 also recovered a foreign-made firearm, a magazine, two bullets and 215 yaba tablets from them.
Local businessmen alleged that one of the arrested men, Mannan, is a known drug dealer and armed criminal who controls drug trading and extortion in the area.
They said businesses cannot operate in the area without paying extortion money.
An unidentified man was found dead on the Airport-bound elevated expressway near Banani around 8:45am on September 4.
The man’s face and both hands were wrapped in Scotch tape, while black marks were visible around his neck.
Police have yet to identify the victim.
According to a source, a bus supervisor noticed a bundle of money while a passenger was paying his fare. The driver and helper allegedly killed the passenger and later dumped his body on the expressway.
In another incident, a man carrying Tk38 lakh after withdrawing the money from a bank was intercepted by three motorcycle-borne criminals in Dhanmondi.
The gang was later arrested with weapons, according to police.
The incidents have fueled concerns among residents and businesspeople as reports of shootings, snatching and killings continue to emerge from different parts of the capital.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police has conducted drives across the capital over the past three days, arresting more than 1,300 people and filing over 150 cases.
Illegal firearms have also been recovered during the drives.
Despite the operations, however, the frequency of violent crimes has raised questions about whether law enforcement efforts are succeeding in containing crime.
DMP Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed told Dhaka Tribune on Sunday evening that DB, CTTC, intelligence and plainclothes police teams were working round the clock to maintain security.
He said the number of police checkposts in the city had been increased from 34 to 81.
“An all-out effort is being made to keep the city safe,” the commissioner said, adding that law enforcement agencies were being deployed immediately after incidents and investigations were being conducted quickly.
Dr Md Omar Faruk, a professor at the Department of Criminology and Police Science at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University, said the growing incidents of snatching, public shootings, extortion and killings were creating fear and anxiety among city residents.
He said economic instability was one of the factors behind the rise in snatching, while criminal syndicates were becoming increasingly organized.
“Snatching was previously mostly carried out by drug addicts, but now organized syndicates are operating in specific areas,” he said.
He also alleged that some police, local political figures and other influential members of society were involved in criminal activities, making it difficult to effectively control crime.
Dr Faruk said police needed research-based crime prevention plans and improved training and professionalism.
He said the police force had yet to fully recover from the disruption following August 5, adding that restoring professionalism and public confidence was essential.
“If the police become professional, they can do everything,” he said.
Meanwhile, RAB has launched cross-country motorcycle patrols in Adabor, Mohammadpur and Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in response to the recent rise in snatching.
RAB-2 ASP Sourav Mahmud said the patrols began on Saturday night and would continue regularly from 9pm to 5am.
He said the initiative was aimed at strengthening nighttime security and creating fear among snatchers operating in the areas.

item.title: JU students lock admin building over 4-point demands
item.description:
Students of A F M Kamaluddin Hall at Jahangirnagar University (JU) locked the main gate of the university’s administrative building on Sunday, protesting over what they described as prolonged delays in renovating the hall’s playground and improving its internal infrastructure.
The students began their sit-in around noon to press home their four-point demand. In protest against the administration’s alleged negligence, they also played cricket in front of the administrative building.
The administrative building remained locked until at least 2 pm, according to the latest information.
The students said the hall’s only playground was damaged during the expansion of the university’s Central Library. Although the administration had promised to renovate the field after the construction work was completed, the commitment has remained unfulfilled for the past three to four years.
Their four-point demands include renovating the fourth-floor roof and installing tiles in 19 rooms, constructing internal connecting roads, immediately renovating the playground, and restoring the barbed-wire security fencing around the hall.
Earlier, on August 27, the hall’s student representatives submitted a memorandum to the vice-chancellor demanding implementation of their demands. They boycotted an administrative coordination meeting, describing it as a “mere formality and a delaying tactic,” and issued an ultimatum for the demands to be met by September 3.

item.title: 334 dengue patients hospitalized in Khulna division in 24 hours
item.description:
A total of 334 dengue patients were hospitalized across Khulna division in the past 24 hours, the highest number of daily patients recorded so far this year.
The information was disclosed in the report issued by the Office of the Divisional Director of Health on Sunday.
According to the report, 7,143 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals across the division between January 1 and September 6. Of them, 21 have died, while 6,112 have recovered and been discharged. Currently, 885 patients are undergoing treatment at different hospitals, while 165 patients have so far been referred elsewhere.
Divisional Health Director Dr Sheikh Md Mosharraf Hossain said 287 of the 334 newly admitted patients were admitted to government hospitals, while 47 were admitted to private facilities.
District-wise data showed that 164 dengue patients were admitted in Khulna in the past 24 hours. Of them, 117 were admitted to government hospitals and 47 to private hospitals. Another 45 patients were admitted to Khulna Medical College Hospital.
Besides, 19 new patients were admitted in Bagerhat, 37 in Jessore, 16 in Jhenaidah, nine in Satkhira, six at Satkhira Medical College Hospital, 14 in Magura, nine in Kushtia, two in Meherpur, six in Narail and seven in Chuadanga.

item.title: Flyover work stalled in Dhamrai, mounting commuter suffering
item.description:
The construction work of a flyover at Kawalipara Bazar in Dhamrai has remained stalled for several months, leaving commuters and local residents to suffer from worsening traffic congestion and poor road conditions.
The flyover was planned to ease congestion at the busy market and improve connectivity. The construction work began in late 2023 under the Tangail-Delduar-Lauhati Road Development Project.
Work initially progressed at a brisk pace but has remained suspended for several months. The construction has narrowed the main road, while numerous potholes have made traffic movement even more difficult.
The road turns muddy and waterlogged after even light rain, while dust creates additional problems during dry weather, causing significant inconvenience to commuters and local residents.
Local residents said vehicles move slowly through the area because of the narrowed road and potholes, resulting in long traffic tailbacks almost every day.
Rajan Ahmed, a resident of Madarpur in Balia union who regularly travels along the road, said congestion at Kawalipara can be severe. “Sometimes it takes us one to one and a half hours just to get through the traffic jam,” he said.
Suman Ahmed, a resident of Nandeshwari, urged the authorities concerned to complete the project quickly. “We want the work to be completed as soon as possible so that we can be free from this daily traffic ordeal,” he said.
According to the Manikganj Roads and Highways Department, the main structure of the flyover has already been completed. However, work on the approach and service roads has been delayed due to administrative complications over land acquisition.
Engineer Shahriar Alam of the department said the land acquisition process is currently underway at the Dhaka Deputy Commissioner’s office. “Once the land acquisition process is completed and the required land is handed over to us, the approach road can be completed. The flyover can then be opened to traffic,” he said.
Residents and regular commuters hope the land acquisition issues will be resolved soon and the remaining work completed without further delay, easing the long-standing congestion and commuting problems at Kawalipara Bazar.

item.title: Indonesia’s main airport suspends operations after volcanic eruption
item.description:
TOPSHOT-INDONESIA-VOLCANO

About 170,000 passengers were left stranded on Sunday as Indonesia shuttered its main international airport and seven others, cancelling hundreds of flights after Mount Anak Krakatoa spewed a plume of volcanic ash and lava from more than 150 kilometres away.

Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement.

Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to suspend operations, the ministry said.

The suspension was extended until 8:59 am Monday “due to increased eruptive activity at Mount Anak Krakatoa”, the airport authority said in an Instagram post.

Operations were also suspended at seven other airports until 8:59 am, authorities said on Instagram. These include the Husein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the ministry said.

“To date, 1,558 flights have been delayed at the eight affected airports, with 170,000 passengers stranded,” the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.

More than 900 affected flights were to and from the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, it added.

Several airports in cities including Semarang and Surabaya have been prepared as alternatives for landing, Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.

Passengers scrambling

The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights.

Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her hometown with her mother, said “everybody was disappointed”.

“No one flew into a rage because, after all, this is due to natural disaster,” the businesswoman who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday told AFP.

Samuel Guiberteau, a Danone executive on a business trip to Lombok since Friday, said “nothing is certain for the moment”, as he searched for alternative flights back to the capital.

“I had found another flight on Citilink, but it was also cancelled,” the 47-year-old told AFP by phone, adding that he had no alternative but to stay in Lombok for the time being.

Volcanic ash also reached the city of Bandar Lampung in the southern tip of Sumatra, blanketing parked cars and roadsides.

“I’m worried it could seriously affect the lungs and cause a lung infection,” Andre Bayu Saputra, 25, told AFP on Sunday.

Schools across Jakarta will be closed on Monday as classes move online, the city said in a statement, without specifying how long the measure will be in place.

Hazard warning

Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.

Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities.

Vessels are prohibited from approaching an exclusion zone of three kilometres radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.

The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.

That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed.

Geology agency head Lana Saria said “seismic activity indicates the movement or release of volcanic fluids within the volcanic system”.

“However, the timing, magnitude, and nature of the next eruption cannot be precisely predicted,” Lana added.

Lana warned against approaching Anak Krakatoa, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone.

She said the most recent series of eruptions do not have the potential to trigger a tsunami at this time.

A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatoa killed 429 people and left thousands displaced.

Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

item.title: 481 killed in road crashes in August, up from July
item.description:
A total of 513 road crashes across the country in August left 481 people dead and 664 injured. The dead included 61 women and 58 children. Motorcycles accounted for 36.59 per cent of all road deaths, with 176 people killed in motorcycle crashes.

These figures were reported by the Road Safety Foundation in its monthly report for August. The organisation compiled the report based on information from nine national dailies, 17 national and regional online news portals, various electronic media outlets and its own data.

The report said 183 motorcycle crashes occurred in August, accounting for 35.67 per cent of all road crashes. In addition, 102 pedestrians were killed, representing 21.20 per cent of the total deaths. Sixty-seven vehicle drivers and assistants were also killed.

By road type, regional roads recorded the highest number of crashes in August, with 217. There were 163 crashes on national highways, 62 on rural roads and 71 on roads in urban areas.

An analysis of the types of crashes showed that 195 occurred after vehicles lost control. Another 126 were head-on collisions, 106 involved pedestrians being run over or hit, and 78 involved vehicles crashing into the backs of other vehicles. Eight crashes occurred for other reasons.

Among the divisions, Dhaka recorded the highest number of crashes, with 172 incidents resulting in 144 deaths. Barishal recorded the lowest, with 15 crashes and 14 deaths. Among individual districts, Bogura recorded the highest number of deaths, at 37. In the capital, 48 crashes left 23 people dead and 54 injured.

An average of 15.51 people were killed in road crashes every day in August. The daily average in July was 13.41 deaths. By that measure, fatalities increased by 15.65 per cent in August.

Road Safety Foundation Executive Director Saidur Rahman said excessive speed was one of the major causes of crashes. Other factors included defective vehicles and roads, reckless attitudes and lack of skills among drivers, long working hours, slow-moving vehicles on highways, reckless motorcycle riding by young people, violations of traffic laws and weak traffic management.

To reduce road crashes, the organisation has recommended technology-based speed monitoring, driver training, removal of unfit and expired vehicles from the roads, initiatives to develop skilled drivers, safer road design and the appointment of gatekeepers at railway crossings. It also emphasised the need for extensive campaigns to raise awareness among road users.

item.title: Class XI admission: Special quota for four categories, including expatriates’ children
item.description:
New guidelines have been issued on admitting students under special quotas to Class XI for the 2026–27 academic year.

Children of expatriates, students with special needs, students who have graduated from the Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Pratisthan (BKSP), and students who have received awards for outstanding contributions to sports and cultural activities at the divisional or national level will be eligible to apply under the quota.

Applications must be submitted manually.

Class-XI admission begins, students can apply to minimum 5 and maximum 10 colleges

The information was disclosed in a letter issued by the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee on Sunday (6 September 2026).

The letter said that, for admission to Class XI under the special quota in the 2026–27 academic year, only students who passed the SSC examination as students with special needs will be able to apply manually for admission to the relevant education board.

Children of expatriates, BKSP graduates, and students who have received awards for outstanding contributions to sports or cultural activities at the divisional or national level may also apply manually to the board for admission.

College admission applications open: How to apply

Meanwhile, online applications for Class XI admission for the 2026–27 academic year began last Wednesday (2 September 2026) and will remain open until 10 September 2026. Classes will begin on 23 September after the admission process is completed.

Students can apply online by following the full guidelines provided on the admission website. Depending on their eligibility, a student can apply to a minimum of five and a maximum of 10 colleges or equivalent educational institutions. The application fee is Tk 220.

item.title: Nepal tunnel rescues face "unprecedented" challenge
item.description:
NEPAL-DISASTER-FLOOD

Nepal’s flood disaster posed an unprecedented challenge, Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix said Monday, with multiple search operations underway in Himalayan hydropower tunnels.

The 26 August glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,385 people, with more than 5,500 missing across the two countries.

Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, with rescue efforts now in their thirteenth day.

“We are facing something I have never faced before,” said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.

“Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved.”

Nepal is holding a national day of mourning on Monday in line with traditional Hindu rituals.

But rescue efforts continue “with the same tempo we had on day one”, Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP on Monday.

“Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels—on ground, by air, and in the tunnels. We are making sure that no one is still stranded.”

The rescue of three workers from deep inside tunnels—two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday—buoyed hopes of finding other survivors.

Foreign experts, including from China, India, and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams in rescue efforts—among them Dix.

“We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon,” said Dix, a key adviser during the Indian rescue of 41 men trapped for 17 days inside the collapsed Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand state in 2023.

“Silkyara taught me never to confuse unlikely with impossible,” he said.

item.title: Shahbagh’s Shaheed Zia Shishu Park may reopen next June after 8 years
item.description:
Shaheed Zia Shishu Park in capital’s Shahbagh, has been closed for nearly eight years. After a long wait, the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) hopes to open the park to the public by June next year.

However, the original timeframe of the project under which the park is being modernised has already expired. Meanwhile, only 30 per cent of the physical work has been completed so far.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of Pubali Bank PLC’s ‘Shishu Park Branch’ at the park project site on Sunday afternoon, DSCC administrator Md Abdus Salam said they hoped to open the park to the public by 30 June 2027.

Dhaka Shishu Park: Costs leap from Tk 780m to Tk 6.06b at Taposh's behest

Abdus Salam said the current government had taken initiatives to complete the remaining work on the park quickly.

He said, “The physical progress of the project currently stands at 30 per cent. An international tender has already been invited to purchase 15 state-of-the-art rides for children’s entertainment.

These rides account for around 75 per cent of the entire project. I hope we will be able to give children a modern park within the stipulated timeframe.”

The nearly 15-acre park in Shahbagh has been closed since January 2019. An underground car park was built beneath the park as part of the third phase of the construction of the Swadhinata Stambha at Suhrawardy Udyan.

Many of the old rides were removed during this work. The park has not reopened for children since then.

Later, the DSCC undertook a Tk 6.03 billion (603.81 crore) project to modernise the park. The project was approved at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) in August 2023.

Its implementation period was from July 2023 to June 2026. Although that deadline has passed, the work is still incomplete.

Of the project’s total cost, Tk 4.83 billion (483 crore) is to be provided by the government and Tk 1.2 billion (120 crore) from the DSCC’s own funds. The largest allocation has been set aside for purchasing and installing 15 rides, with around Tk 4.41 billion (441 crore) earmarked for this.

Dhaka children’s park: Modernisation stalls, weeds take over

At the event, Abdus Salam called on private organisations to use their corporate social responsibility funds to participate in cleanliness drives, beautification and tree planting as part of efforts to develop Dhaka as a ‘clean city, green city’.

He also urged people to keep their homes and surrounding areas clean to prevent dengue and ensure that water does not remain stagnant anywhere for more than three days.

Pubali Bank PLC Managing Director and Chief Executive Mohammad Ali, along with officials from the DSCC and the bank, attended the event.

item.title: What is a 'ruined economy' to the finance adviser
item.description:
On 28 August, during Ekattor TV's 'Business Weekend' programme, presenter Iqbal Ahsan interviewed the government's advisor on financial and planning matters. In the interview, the finance advisor strongly claimed that all current crises were created by the fallen government. He further claimed that this government is supposedly cleaning up the mess left by the past.

The advisor is a professor of development economics. However, he brought Rabindranath into his argument by saying, “Whatever is lost, the mistress of the house says 'Keshta is the thief'. He stated that no crisis is contemporary; they are all accumulated crises. In that case, no development is contemporary either; all are offerings from the past.

Economic history teaches us that past governance can indeed be blamed for a current crisis. But the rule of the fallen Awami government ended two years ago. Did the crisis then skip over the interim Yunus government and land solely on the BNP’s shoulders? Shouldn't the Awami League's crisis have fallen on Yunus's government? The advisor did not mention anything about the one-and-a-half-year interim rule.

The finance minister himself, however, acknowledged that the 18 months of governance further devastated the economy. The data supports this. Both investment and growth have decreased in the face of high inflation and high unemployment. One cannot hope for better during the golden age of mobocracy. Yet, the finance advisor made a giant leap to 2024-2026.

This GDP is now planned by the BNP government to be transformed into a trillion-dollar economy by 2034. If 450 billion is equated with devastation, then we are in trouble. Development is a cumulatively promising process. Recognizing the good and bad of the past is a sign of intellectual courtesy.

In 1958, Chinese leader Mao Zedong introduced the theory of the great leap in the country's industrialisation. It holds historical value. But will the Finance Adviser's 'temporal leap theory'—offered to shift the blame—hold any real weight? Another advisor gained fame by theorising that no blame for the current energy crisis should fall on the current government. With advisors increasingly stirring the field with their political statements, the future seems bleak for members of parliament.

Waiting for a cautious economy

In the interview, the finance advisor repeatedly mentioned that they have inherited a ‘devastated’ economy. If a leader at the district or sub-district level had made such a statement, I wouldn’t have felt compelled to respond. But when a teacher of economics at Dhaka University repeatedly uses the word ‘devastated’ without understanding its definition, it must mean that the government wants to hear this narrative from socially recognised scholars.

Dr. Debapriya Bhattacharya, a distinguished fellow of CPD, questioned this use of the word ‘devastated'. He demanded documentation from the government to support this claim. This government should have started work by composing a ‘review’ of the state of the post-COVID economy over the past five years. It could have included both the Awami and Yunus governments. There would be no need to speak from old white papers.

Those who have previously worked for free on white papers might have still worked if invited. Perhaps the government refrained from this ‘stocktaking’ task for fear of offending the scholars of the Yunus government. They abruptly started work without proper homework. Taking this opportunity, advisors are following the ‘Wolf and the Lamb’ story, providing one ‘blame theory’ after another. None of these have any basis in data.

If we search Google or ask AI for examples of a devastated economy, four primary national examples arise: 1. The Great Depression in the United States, 2. Hyperinflation in 1920s Germany, 3. The catastrophic famine during the Great Leap Forward in China from 1958 to 1962, and 4. The Argentine crisis from 1998 to 2002.

The main indicators of devastation here are massive GDP contraction and famine. In some cases, GDP contracted by up to 30 per cent. That means those countries experienced negative GDP growth, which has never happened in Bangladesh’s 50-year history. So, by what theory did the advisor discover this ‘economic devastation’? Is there a separate definition of a devastated economy in development economics?

After the fall of the Ershad government, from 1991 onwards, Bangladesh entered a new era of market economy and growth. According to the World Bank, in these 35 years from then to today, Bangladesh’s average growth has been 5.5 per cent, which is the second-highest in South Asia. Only five years during this time saw GDP growth dip into the 3 per cent range.

These years were - 1. The first year of BNP in power, i. e. , 1991, 2. Another year of the same tenure, 1994, 3. The start of another BNP tenure, i. e. , 2002, 4. The COVID year under Awami rule, 2020, and 5. The year 2025 under Yunus’s rule. Even in these years of poor growth, did any economist say that the economy had collapsed?

Apart from 1971, no year in Bangladesh's history has seen a devastated economy. Growth then had fallen to a negative 5.5 per cent, and in 1972 it dropped to negative 14 per cent, which remains the worst contraction in Bangladesh’s history. After the genocide and destruction of infrastructure by the Pakistani army, this record drop in growth was not unusual. By that measure, if the current advisor were narrating the story of a devastated economy in 1973, it would have a documentary basis.

In the last year of Awami rule, in 2024, growth was 4.22 per cent, yet during their 16 years from 2009-2024, Bangladesh’s average growth was 6.16 per cent. Where are the signs of devastation here? Many malpractices have occurred in the economy under Awami rule, especially in the stock market and banking sector.

Economists have spoken and written extensively on that. I have written multiple books myself. But no one has burst out with baseless claims. Researchers must remain objective, not emotional. According to the World Bank, after 2006, BNP left an economy worth 80 billion dollars. Subsequently, Awami League took an economy of nearly 100 billion dollars in 2009 and turned it into a 450 billion dollar economy by 2024. In 2025, GDP reached 456 billion dollars. In 2026, it is estimated to approach 500 billion dollars.

This GDP is now planned by the BNP government to be transformed into a trillion-dollar economy by 2034. If 450 billion is equated with devastation, then we are in trouble. Development is a cumulatively promising process. Recognizing the good and bad of the past is a sign of intellectual courtesy.

What a minister or MP can do or say may not always be appropriate for an advisor. A minister will often highlight the Prime Minister’s statements. In contrast, an advisor should present a data- and knowledge-based analysis, enriching people through research.

#Dr. Birupaksha Paul is an economics professor at the State University of New York at Cortland.

item.title: Luxembourg - The only Grand Duchy on Earth
item.description:
Luxembourg is one of the most beautiful and unique countries in Europe - the world’s only remaining Grand Duchy, where history, elegance, and modern life exist in perfect harmony.

Small in size yet grand in character, Luxembourg offers visitors a rare blend of royal heritage, stunning architecture, peaceful landscapes, and refined European charm.

Nestled in the heart of Europe, Luxembourg enjoys a remarkable strategic location, bordering Belgium, France, and Germany. Its central position has made it an important bridge between European cultures, languages, and economies. Though small in size, Luxembourg carries significant global influence in finance, diplomacy, and international cooperation.

The Grand Duke serves as the Head of State, symbolising the nation’s rich heritage, unity, and constitutional traditions. Despite its royal institution, Luxembourg is also a vibrant parliamentary democracy where elected representatives govern through democratic principles, balancing tradition with modern governance.

Luxembourg City is admired for its breathtaking beauty - from medieval castles and picturesque villages to lush green valleys and charming old towns. Luxembourg City, the capital, blends historic fortifications with modern architecture, creating an atmosphere where history and innovation coexist harmoniously. The nation’s high quality of life, safety, cleanliness, and multicultural environment make it one of the most attractive places to live and visit in Europe.

The famous old quarters and fortifications, recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, reflect centuries of European history and culture. Visitors can walk through charming streets filled with cafés, boutiques, museums, and heritage architecture while enjoying breathtaking views of lush green surroundings.

Luxembourg is also a wonderful travel destination for those who appreciate art, culture, history, and romance. Every season brings a different charm: spring blooms with flowers and greenery, summer fills the terraces and parks with life, autumn paints the valleys in golden colors, and winter transforms the city into a magical European wonderland.

Elegant yet welcoming, historical yet modern, Luxembourg offers travelers a rare experience of serenity, culture, and timeless beauty. It is a country where heritage and nature coexist beautifully, making it one of Europe’s most enchanting destinations.

Luxembourg stands as a symbol of elegance, stability, and progress - a nation where royal legacy, democratic values, and natural beauty come together in perfect harmony.

* Nasreen  Zamir is Honorary Consul of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in Dhaka

item.title: Makkah Defense Alliance: Should Bangladesh step into the quicksand?
item.description:
After World War II, military alliances emerged in various regions as a result of the ideological competition between the Western world and the Soviet Union. But in today’s world, there is no longer competition between two distinct camps, and many regions have no such military alliances.
That is perhaps why the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement has aroused curiosity in many countries. The geographical composition of the Makkah Alliance and the circumstances surrounding its formation have given rise to considerable speculation.
The formal journey of this alliance, comprising Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, began a month ago. On September 1, at the first formal meeting in Istanbul, it was decided to establish a secretariat in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
At the same time, the military and diplomatic leaders of the three countries decided to appoint a Pakistani official as the alliance’s first secretary general for a three-year term.
Following the political decision to form the alliance, the process of establishing its administrative and management structure is now beginning. The easier tasks will come first.
It is expected that the more complex steps required to make a military alliance effective will be taken in the future. However, beyond those complex steps, much remains to be determined -- including the alliance’s ideology, objectives, policies, expansion, and identification of enemies and allies.
It can be said that much more remains unknown about the alliance than is currently known. That is precisely why it has generated so much curiosity among countries outside the grouping.
At the Istanbul meeting, however, officials from the host country made some attempts to satisfy that curiosity, answering some, if not all, of the questions surrounding the alliance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the alliance was created on the basis of international values such as respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states and non-interference in their internal affairs. However, declaring such values is far easier than adhering to them, as even a cursory look at world politics makes clear.
But there is little doubt that the issue of territorial integrity is of considerable importance to the alliance. Just as alliance member Turkey is fighting separatist Kurdish rebels in the southeast of the country, another member, Pakistan, is confronting increasing activity by independence-seeking armed groups in its Balochistan province.
Hakan Fidan said the Makkah Defense Alliance has no enemies and that its doors are open to other countries. “This alliance is not against any one country, and it is open to all those who share our values in our region,” he said.
Fidan said two things in a single sentence about the possible expansion of the alliance.
First, “open to all”, meaning anyone can join. This statement will give hope to those in Bangladesh who are interested in joining the alliance. Bangladesh has not yet been invited to join, but officials in Dhaka have been expressing their interest for several days.
But Fidan also added the words “in our region.” What exactly does he mean by “region” here?
The founding members of the alliance are primarily countries belonging to the West Asia-Persian Gulf-Mediterranean geopolitical space. Bangladesh, on the other hand, belongs to the South-Southeast Asia-Bay of Bengal region.
Regional media reports discussing potential new members of the alliance have more frequently mentioned Egypt and Syria. There is little doubt that Saudi Arabia is interested in bringing Egypt into the alliance, while Turkey wants to bring Syria under its umbrella.
It is difficult to identify any obvious role for Bangladesh in this Middle East-centred security and political framework.
Various local media reports suggest that there are concerns within the alliance about admitting new members. Any new member could bring additional military and political strength.
But it could also introduce different policy priorities, particularly in foreign affairs, as well as different security perspectives -- all of which could complicate the alliance’s operations.
For example, while Bangladesh could contribute experienced peacekeeping troops to the alliance, Dhaka’s geopolitical and strategic priorities would remain focused on Southeast Asia and the Bay of Bengal.
Bangladesh should aim to maintain cordial relations with all countries in West Asia. Participating in a military alliance in the region would mean becoming involved in local disputes, which would run counter to Bangladesh’s interests.
The debate in Dhaka over the alliance is also examining the India factor from two perspectives.
On the one hand, it is being argued that joining the alliance would strengthen Bangladesh’s security and deter India from aggression.
On the other hand, membership could have precisely the opposite effect.
Joining the alliance would mean establishing formal military ties with Pakistan, which could lead India to view Bangladesh as a threat to its security.
It is difficult to understand how a military alliance can be formed without identifying an “enemy.” No matter how “defensive” an alliance claims to be, why would three countries commit themselves to military action in one another’s defense unless they perceived a threat?
The question becomes even more relevant when one of the three countries possesses around 150 nuclear weapons.
The source of the threat has almost certainly been identified. But the secrecy surrounding it suggests that the alliance’s appeal and effectiveness could be undermined if that country or group were publicly named.
Fidan emphasized certain values in his speech, one of which was “non-interference in anyone’s internal affairs.” This principle was probably raised with Iran in mind.
Since the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979, the Gulf Arab countries have complained that Tehran seeks to export its revolution to Arab states. There is little doubt that Iranian revolutionaries wanted to overthrow the monarchical systems of the Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia.
Iraq invaded Iran in 1980 with financial and other support from Arab countries. Saddam Hussein believed that post-revolutionary Iran could be defeated easily. But after eight years of war, Iraq was forced to accept a ceasefire without achieving its objectives.
The question now is whether the Makkah Defense Alliance was created with Iran in mind. From the perspective of Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries, such an assumption would seem natural.
Although Pakistan maintains friendly relations with Iran, Islamabad has been providing troops for Saudi Arabia’s security for decades.
Turkey’s inclusion sends another message. Recent comments by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggest that war between the two countries may only be a matter of time.
Turkey has been expanding its military presence and political influence in Syria over the past year and a half, developments that Israel views as a threat to its security.
Israel’s plan was to establish dominance across the region after destroying Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the Assad regime in Syria. The final obstacle was Iran.
But the failure of the US war against Iran has almost derailed Israel’s plan. Israel is now focused on disarming Syria, but Turkey stands in the way.
The announcement of the alliance comes at a time when the security architecture of the Persian Gulf and eastern Mediterranean has almost collapsed.
The joint US-Israeli military operation aimed at overthrowing the Islamic regime in Iran has effectively failed, creating a security vacuum in the region.
Iran has shattered the perception that the US military presence in the Gulf guarantees the security of Saudi Arabia and other Arab monarchies.
There is considerable uncertainty over when, if ever, US military bases in the Gulf will return. It is believed that the Makkah Defense Alliance will attempt to fill this security vacuum.
The initial assessment is that the alliance is primarily focused on Iran and the Houthi group in Yemen. The main threats to Saudi Arabia’s security come from these two sources.
Israel had hoped to become the principal driving force behind a new regional security architecture following Iran’s defeat. Iran disrupted that plan by calling on Arab countries to coordinate their security with Tehran.
The Makkah Defense Alliance has created the possibility of a new geopolitical alignment in West Asia, in which a regional security architecture could emerge outside the orbit of the United States, Israel, and Iran.
Bangladesh’s ruling authorities probably believe that joining the alliance would not only strengthen the country’s economic interests, particularly manpower exports and energy imports, but also enable Dhaka to play a strategic role in this important region.
But are the interests and perspectives of the alliance’s founding members really the same? No. The same would apply to any new members.
The history of the Middle East teaches us that friendships and enmities rarely remain permanent. Loyalties can shift like the sands of the desert. Bangladesh will have to tread very carefully here, lest it stumble into quicksand.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.
Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Chasing blue skies
item.description:
As the world marks the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, our country is confronted with a sobering truth: Our fight against air pollution is nowhere near where it needs to be.
Bangladesh continues to underestimate the deadly toll of polluted air, even as respiratory illnesses rise, premature deaths increase, and millions of people breathe toxic air every single day.
This day is meant to remind nations that clean air ought to be a fundamental right. For Bangladesh, it should serve as a wake‑up call.
Air pollution has long been one of our most pressing public health emergencies. We consistently rank among the world’s most polluted, with air in our capital and major cities far exceeding safe limits.
Yet, our national response remains fragmented, slow, and often reactive rather than preventive.
From children developing asthma at alarming rates to elderly citizens suffering from chronic diseases to workers needing to work while inhaling air thick with dust, smoke, and chemical emissions, air pollution affects every person but disproportionately affects the marginalized and vulnerable and moves us further away from becoming an equitable nation.
That illegal brick kilns and unregulated factories continue mushrooming is also among our biggest failures, all the while the true number of pollution‑linked deaths remains undercounted, masking the scale of the crisis.
To say we cannot continue down this path would be an understatement. Let today be a reminder that clean air is essential for economic growth, public health, and national stability.
The deadly toll of air pollution is rising, even if official numbers fail to capture its full extent. We must confront this reality with urgency and ambition and recognize that clean air is not a luxury but a necessity if we want to be a healthy, productive, and resilient nation.

item.title: Heeding the call for a liveable environment
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s latest remarks urging collective action for a pollution‑free Bangladesh must be heeded.
Pollution in our country, especially in our major cities, is a daily assault on public health, economic productivity, and the basic livability of our cities. As such, when the head of our government recognizes the issue and calls for unity and urgency, the nation collectively must listen and act.
Of course, our pollution crisis is multidimensional. We have already spoken of our struggling air quality in major cities that routinely falls into hazardous levels in our first editorial, but that is just one aspect of it.
Rivers are choked with industrial waste, sewage, and plastic. Noise pollution has become a constant urban stressor, and unplanned development continues to erode green spaces and natural buffers.
The consequences of this pollution are visible everywhere and affect everyone: rising respiratory illnesses, contaminated water sources, declining biodiversity, and a quality of life that is deteriorating even as the country strives for economic progress.
The prime minister is right to emphasize that this fight cannot be won by the government alone. Pollution is produced by factories that ignore regulations, by corporations that dump waste into canals, by unfit vehicles that belch smoke, and by institutions that treat environmental rules as optional.
A pollution‑free Bangladesh requires responsibility at every level, from policymakers to businesses to ordinary citizens.
A liveable Bangladesh must be the goal, and it is possible only if we treat pollution as the national emergency it is.

item.title: The great digital delusion
item.description:
If you had told a Bangladeshi parent 20 years ago that their child would one day make millions of Taka a month by slapping dye into their hair, dancing wildly on a public overpass, or staging a screaming match with their in-laws in front of a ring light, they would have gently recommended a psychiatric consultation.
Yet, here we are in 2026.
The algorithm is the new deity, the smartphone is the altar, and "views" have somehow become a substitute for value.
Take, for instance, the recent domestic melodrama that dominated our feeds.
The internet exploded with details of infamous TikToker Prince Mamun allegedly joining forces with his second wife to physically assault and evict his own mother and mute sister from their home.
To complete this tragic soap opera, his former partner -- the ever-present "Blue Fairy" Laila -- rushed to the scene to offer shelter to the distressed mother, all under the piercing gaze of rolling smartphones and eager cameras.
Was it genuine heartbreak? Was it an orchestrated PR play? Does anyone even care anymore?
In the hyper-monetized content circus of Bangladesh, human dignity, filial piety, and familial trauma are no longer private matters.
They are mere "hooks" designed to drive retention rates, inflate impressions, and capture ad revenue.
When a society begins to trade its basic moral currency for digital validation, we must pause and ask: Is this truly the "future of work" we were promised?
There was a time when upward social mobility required sweat, late-night study sessions, and decades of professional discipline.
Today, creators like Prince Mamun, Opu Bhai, and Rakib Hossain have bypassed traditional educational paths entirely.
Armed with little more than raw charisma, sensationalism, and an uncanny ability to exploit digital algorithms, these individuals have accumulated fortunes that leave university graduates, engineers, and corporate executives scratching their heads in utter disbelief.
Seeing unlettered influencers pull in tens of thousands of dollars a month while a fresh graduate earns peanuts at an entry-level job has created a profound psychological rift among Bangladeshi youth.
Why endure 16 years of grueling academic pressure only to face a stagnating job market when you can buy a tripod, film a provocative vlog, and land a lucrative brand deal by next Tuesday?
Thousands of young Bangladeshis are abandoning classrooms and technical institutions, harbouring a dangerous ambition: To become "content creators."
They mistake temporary digital notoriety for a legitimate career, unaware that building a life on social media metrics is like building a house on shifting sand.
This entitlement to unearned wealth and status -- where one expects to enjoy all the rewards of social prominence without first putting in the sweat, integrity, or moral dues -- recently manifested in yet another grim headline.
Content creator Ripon Miah, who amassed nearly 1.9 million Facebook followers on the back of quick social media clips, was recently arrested by law enforcement after being accused of abusing his influencer status to harass and ultimately rape a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Netrakona.
Media reports revealed how local influential figures initially attempted to "settle" the heinous crime through an illegal local arbitration ( shalish ), fining him Tk5 lakh and asking him to leave the village while video clips of his apology went viral online.
Ripon’s trajectory -- from a local carpenter to a viral celebrity, and ultimately an accused predator attempting to buy his way out of criminal accountability with easy social media money -- serves as a chilling reminder of what happens when massive influence and financial windfalls precede character, discipline, and hard-earned merit.
It is the ultimate manifestation of wanting to pocket the rewards of success without paying the fundamental dues of human decency, rule of law, and honest labor first.
What these aspiring influencers fail to realize is that content creation is fundamentally unsustainable.
Relevance in the "reel-scrolling" era is ruthlessly ephemeral.
The same audience that elevates an influencer to digital royalty today will swipe away tomorrow without a second thought.
A single change in an algorithm, a shift in audience tastes, or a temporary suspension of monetization can instantly reduce a "social media millionaire" to complete financial oblivion.
Worse still, this desperate race for virality has given birth to a sinister, predatory ecosystem.
The promise of social media fame is no longer just a distraction -- it has turned into a dangerous trap.
Media reports across Bangladesh have documented tragic instances where young girls from vulnerable backgrounds were lured with promises of becoming "TikTok stars" or landed roles in viral videos.
Instead, they faced horrific fates -- abduction, sexual assault, and human trafficking networks operating under the guise of talent agencies and creator houses.
The tragic reality is that while a select few pocket cash from ad networks, scores of impressionable youths pay for this illusion with their lives, freedom, and dignity.
Even for those who manage to stay on the legitimate side of the law, the golden goose of online monetization is growing tired.
Platform giants like YouTube continuously refine their Partner Program policies.
In their ongoing efforts to appease advertisers, platforms are cracking down on repetitive content, sensationalized clickbait, low-effort clips, and ethical violations.
For Bangladeshi creators reliant on sensationalism or repurposed content, the revenue gravy train is slowing down.
While YouTube periodically adjusts regional monetization pathways, making it technically easier for localized content to earn revenue, the bar for qualifying content is rising sharply.
Algorithms are increasingly penalizing vulgarity, family drama, and synthetic outrage.
When the platforms decide to clean up their digital storefronts, hundreds of creators who traded their education for short-term views will find themselves with neither a steady paycheck nor transferable skills for the real world.
This brings us to an inescapable truth: Mobile-generated content can never ethically or practically replace real labour, technical expertise, and formal education.
A nation cannot run on reaction videos, pranks, and unboxing clips.
Who will design the bridges, manage the power grids, or write the software systems that keep our economy moving forward?
Who will treat the sick, harvest the crops, teach the next generation, or manufacture the very goods that influencers unbox on camera?
True labor builds tangible value. It instills discipline, produces tangible progress, and offers a level of personal self-respect that no amount of digital "likes" can ever match.
Formal and technical education are not merely decorative certificates but are the structural framework of a functional society.
They impart problem-solving capabilities, critical thinking, and resilient skills that withstand algorithmic shifts, economic downturns, and platform updates.
There is no shame in leveraging modern technology to express oneself, share stories, or build an audience.
But when content creation degrades into public spectacles of familial abuse -- where a mother's tears are treated as engagement fuel -- it ceases to be entertainment.
It becomes a sign of moral degradation masquerading as entrepreneurship.
We must strip away the illusion surrounding "influencer culture."
Let the youth enjoy their short-form videos, but let them also understand the clear line between a temporary hobby and a lifelong profession.
Real success is not measured in subscriber counts, brand deals, or viral scandals.
It is measured in the quiet dignity of honest work, the pursuit of real knowledge, and the enduring strength of human integrity.
In the end, when the screens go black and the servers shut down, it is honest, physical, and intellectual labor that will keep the world turning -- long after the last reel has been swiped away.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: What you can do to combat dengue
item.description:
Bangladesh is no longer facing dengue as a simple seasonal disease. It has evolved into a complex public health challenge influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, environmental degradation, changing human behavior, and weaknesses in vector control systems.
The alarming rise in dengue cases over the past several years clearly indicates that traditional approaches are no longer sufficient. Dengue prevention and control must now be viewed as a national development priority rather than merely a health-sector responsibility. The changing epidemiology of dengue in Bangladesh demands a fundamental shift in strategy.
Climate change isn't just altering ecosystems but actively reshaping infectious disease boundaries and elevating the spillover and epidemic risks of neglected, rare pathogens. Climate change has significantly altered the pattern of mosquito-borne diseases worldwide, and Bangladesh is among the countries most vulnerable to its consequences.
Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, prolonged monsoon seasons, waterlogging, floods, and increasing humidity have created ideal conditions for the breeding and survival of Aedes mosquitoes. Previously, dengue transmission was largely concentrated between June and September. However, recent outbreaks have demonstrated that the transmission season has expanded beyond traditional boundaries.
Unpredictable weather patterns are allowing mosquitoes to reproduce more rapidly and survive for longer periods. Urban flooding creates countless artificial breeding sites, while warmer temperatures accelerate both mosquito development and viral replication.
Therefore, climate change adaptation strategies must be integrated into Bangladesh's dengue control policies. Public health authorities should collaborate closely with meteorological agencies, urban planners, environmental experts, and local government institutions to develop climate-informed dengue forecasting models.
One of the greatest misconceptions in Bangladesh is the belief that fogging alone can control dengue.
Fogging primarily targets adult mosquitoes and often provides only temporary relief. However, Aedes mosquitoes reproduce in small collections of clean, stagnant water found inside homes, on rooftops, in flowerpots, in discarded containers, on construction sites, in water storage facilities, etc.
The most effective intervention remains the destruction of mosquito breeding sites. Vector control should become a year-round activity rather than an emergency response implemented only after case numbers begin to rise.
Dengue control ultimately depends on human behavior. The Aedes mosquito is predominantly a household mosquito and breeds in domestic environments and usually bites during the daytime.
Simple behavioral changes can dramatically reduce mosquito breeding:
Unfortunately, many people continue to view dengue prevention as the sole responsibility of city corporations. This mindset must change. Behavioral change communication should become a continuous national campaign.
Bangladesh must fully adopt integrated vector management (IVM) as the foundation of its dengue prevention strategy.
IVM is a comprehensive approach that combines:
Instead of conducting indiscriminate insecticide spraying, resources should be directed toward identifying mosquito breeding hotspots through entomological surveillance and geographic information system (GIS)-based mapping.
Integrated vector management also requires close coordination among the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, city corporations, municipalities, educational institutions, the Ministry of Local Government, the Department of Environment, and urban development authorities. Dengue is not simply a medical problem; it is an environmental and governance challenge.
No country has successfully controlled dengue without active community participation. Community engagement should move beyond awareness campaigns and evolve into community ownership. Neighborhood-based clean-up campaigns, school health programs, youth volunteer initiatives, and community surveillance teams can significantly reduce mosquito breeding sites.
A nationwide weekly "Dengue Clean Day" could become an effective public health intervention. Local communities should be encouraged to inspect their homes and surroundings regularly and report potential breeding sites to local authorities. Bangladesh's own dengue strategy recognizes community participation as the key to sustainable dengue control.
Rapid and often unplanned urbanization has transformed many areas of Bangladesh into favourable environments for Aedes mosquitoes. Blocked drainage systems, indiscriminate waste disposal, plastic containers, abandoned tires, rooftop water accumulation, and poorly managed construction projects continue to create ideal breeding habitats. Environmental sanitation should therefore become an integral component of dengue prevention.
Priority actions should include:
The responsibility for environmental sanitation extends far beyond the health sector. Urban planners, engineers, municipal authorities, construction companies, and communities must work together to reduce environmental risks. Bangladesh's current guidance specifically highlights waste management and sanitation as critical components of dengue prevention.
Every year, hospitals become overwhelmed when dengue cases begin to surge. This reactive approach must be replaced by proactive preparedness.
Institutional readiness should include:
Health facilities should begin preparing before the onset of the monsoon rather than waiting for patient numbers to increase. Early diagnosis and appropriate case management remain the most effective ways to reduce dengue-related deaths. These preparedness measures are also emphasized in national recommendations.
The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends the use of the dengue vaccine Qdenga® (TAK-003) for children aged 6-16 years living in areas with high dengue transmission intensity.
Importantly, vaccination should never replace traditional prevention measures. WHO clearly states that dengue vaccines should be implemented as part of a comprehensive dengue control strategy.
One of the most important lessons from recent dengue outbreaks is that surveillance systems must become more predictive.
Traditional case reporting alone is insufficient. Bangladesh requires an integrated early warning system that combines:
A modern surveillance system should identify high-risk areas before outbreaks occur rather than simply documenting cases after transmission has already intensified.
Effective surveillance can provide policy-makers with the information needed to deploy resources, strengthen vector control, and prepare health facilities in advance. National strategies already emphasize real-time reporting, hotspot mapping, and early warning systems.
Bangladesh continues to repeat the same mistake every year by initiating dengue control activities after the arrival of the monsoon. This approach must change. Seasonal preparedness should begin at least two to three months before the rainy season and include:
Dengue control activities should follow an annual preparedness calendar rather than an emergency response model. Current guidance recommends that control activities begin before the peak transmission season.
Bangladesh has successfully addressed many major public health challenges through strong political commitment and multisectoral collaboration. Dengue should be approached in the same way.
The country needs a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach that brings together:
The fight against dengue requires behavioral change, environmental responsibility, scientific surveillance, climate adaptation, institutional preparedness, and community ownership.
Dengue is no longer merely a seasonal outbreak. It is a warning signal about the intersection of climate change, urbanization, environmental neglect, and public health vulnerability.
Dr M Salim Uzzaman is a public health specialist & strategist (expert: EIDs, disease surveillance, One Health, and global health security).

item.title: Shykh Seraj turns 73, marking four decades in development journalism
item.description:
Prominent agricultural development and media personality Shykh Seraj turns 73 on Monday, marking more than four decades of work in development journalism and agriculture-focused broadcasting.
Born in Chandpur on September 7, 1954, Seraj earned his master’s degree in geography from the University of Dhaka.
He became involved in media during his student years and later gained widespread recognition through Bangladesh Television’s popular agriculture programme “Mati O Manush”.
At Channel i, he went on to launch the pioneering agriculture-based programme “Hridoye Mati O Manush”.
His “Chhad Krishi” initiative, aimed at encouraging urban residents to take up rooftop farming, has since grown into a wider social movement.
Over more than four decades in the media, Seraj has brought farmers and often-overlooked agricultural issues into mainstream national discourse.
His reporting and awareness campaigns have also contributed to efforts to advance food production and modern agricultural practices in Bangladesh, establishing him as a pioneer of development journalism.
In recognition of his contributions, Seraj received two of Bangladesh’s highest state honours -- the Ekushey Padak in 1995 and the Independence Award in 2018.
He received the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations’ A H Boerma Award in 2009 for his contribution to food security and poverty alleviation.
Seraj has received more than 50 awards and honours at home and abroad, including the Gusi Peace Prize and a special honour from the British House of Commons.
He currently serves as founding director and head of news at Impress Telefilm Limited and Channel i.
Seraj has also authored several books on agriculture and development. His body of television work has drawn academic attention as well, with a PhD research project examining his contribution completed at the University of Dhaka.
