item.title: Mirpur businesses squeezed by multiple criminal groups
item.description:
Businesses across greater Mirpur are facing extortion demands from at least five criminal groups, with traders and entrepreneurs allegedly being forced to pay multiple groups operating in the same areas.
The groups have established networks across Mirpur, Pallabi and Rupnagar, targeting businesses ranging from dish and internet services, bus stands and rickshaw garages to housing projects, restaurants and markets. Those who refuse to pay allegedly face threats, shootings and attacks.
At the centre of the growing extortion network is the Five Star group, whose alleged top leaders are abroad but whose followers continue to operate locally. Intelligence sources cited in the report estimate that the group has at least 2,000 followers on the ground.
The group was previously known as Four Star but is now being referred to as Five Star following the emergence of Ashik, leader of the teenage gang “Bhoi-ra De,” according to local sources.
The alleged top leaders of the group are Mamun, Shahadat, Ibrahim and Moktar. Intelligence information says Mamun is in Malaysia, Ibrahim in France, Shahadat in Italy and Moktar in India, while Ashik is reportedly in Nepal.
Despite being abroad, the alleged leaders are said to be running their networks through associates in Mirpur using mobile applications, encrypted calls, WhatsApp and VoIP services.
According to intelligence information, at least 150 active cadres are involved in field-level operations for the group.
Mamun has been identified as a listed fugitive convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. He has at least 27 cases against him involving allegations of extortion, murder, drug trading, arms and robbery, according to the report.
His alleged associates include Jamilur Rahman, Mashiur Rahman, Delwar Hossain Rubel, Nata Alamgir, Kala Motaleb, Rajon, Sunny and Langra Rubel.
A number of audio clips allegedly containing extortion demands, threats and disputes over the collection of money have recently gone viral.
In one such clip, Ashik is allegedly heard demanding Tk50 lakh from a businessman and saying project work would have to stop if the money was not paid.
When the businessman says another group has already collected money from him, Ashik allegedly responds that it is not his concern who took the money.
Local businesses say they are increasingly being caught between competing criminal groups, with some allegedly having to pay more than one group operating in the same area.
A resident, Arafat, alleged that shootings in Pallabi have taken place over extortion disputes and that demands for money were also linked to shooting incidents in Kafrul and Rupnagar.
Another resident, Sujon, said groups linked to Mamun and Ashik have a strong presence in Pallabi, Kalshi and Baunia.
He alleged that people who pay one group are subsequently approached by another group for money, while those who refuse can face shootings or attacks with machetes.
The extortion disputes have also intensified territorial conflicts among the groups, contributing to frequent shootings in Mirpur, Pallabi and Rupnagar, according to residents.
Mirpur division Deputy Commissioner Tanvir Sarkar, RAB-4 Additional SP K N Niyoti Roy and DMP Detective Branch chief Shafiqul Islam have spoken about the criminal networks and law enforcement efforts in the area, according to the report.
The authorities say law enforcement agencies are working to identify and take action against those involved in criminal activities and extortion.
For businesses in greater Mirpur, however, the problem remains a daily reality, with competing groups allegedly demanding payments and leaving traders caught between the threat of paying and the risk of retaliation.

item.title: ‘No shortage’, yet farmers scramble for fertiliser
item.description:
Fertiliser tensions are spreading across farming districts, with farmers blocking a major highway in Rajshahi and breaking into a dealer’s warehouse in Kurigram on Monday, exposing a widening gap between government assurances of adequate stocks and farmers’ claims that fertiliser is either unavailable or being sold at inflated prices.
In Kurigram alone, unrest has now surfaced in Roumari, Bhurungamari and Nageshwari, while around 300 farmers in Rajshahi blocked the Dhaka-Rajshahi highway for about an hour, demanding adequate supplies and action against what they described as a syndicate creating an artificial shortage.
The protests come at a critical stage of the Aman season, when farmers say delays in fertiliser application could affect crops.
Agriculture officials and dealers, however, insist there is no overall shortage -- raising questions over whether the crisis lies in national supply or in distribution, access and pricing at the local level.
The most dramatic scenes unfolded at a fertiliser dealer point in Roumari, Kurigram, where farmers who had gathered since early morning broke through the tin fence and entered the warehouse after distribution failed to begin on time.
Eyewitnesses said more than 100 sacks were taken away, some carried on farmers’ heads and others transported by autorickshaw and van. Videos of the incident circulated on social media.
Dealer manager Saiful Islam acknowledged that farmers broke into the warehouse and took fertiliser while staff had gone to seek assistance from the administration.
He said some sacks were later returned, abandoned beside the road or paid for.
According to him, 739 sacks were in the warehouse at the time and there was no shortage.
The local administration disputed descriptions of the incident as looting.
Roumari Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Mahbubul Hasan said there had been some disorder but maintained that farmers queued to buy fertiliser and returned after law enforcement brought the situation under control.
Hours later, farmers demonstrated again in Bhurungamari, blocking a road with bamboo and setting it on fire after allegedly failing to obtain fertiliser.
The contradiction between farmers and officials was laid bare by Bhurungamari Police Station Officer-in-Charge Azim Uddin.
“Farmers have protested because they have not received fertilizer. The Agriculture Department says there is no shortage of fertilizer. But farmers say they are not receiving fertilizer. If there is fertilizer, why can’t farmers get it?” he said.
Kurigram Department of Agricultural Extension Deputy Director Abdullah Al Mamun insisted supplies were sufficient for seasonal demand.
He suggested rumours were prompting some farmers to buy additional fertiliser in advance and said authorities were examining whether a third party could be fuelling the unrest.
In Rajshahi, frustration brought traffic on the Dhaka-Rajshahi highway to a standstill.
Around 300 farmers blocked the highway at Baneshwar in Puthia at about 10am after waiting in queues for fertiliser.
Hundreds of vehicles were stranded before the blockade was withdrawn following assurances from the local administration.
Farmers alleged that dealers were telling them fertiliser was unavailable at government-set prices while supplies could be obtained from retailers by paying more.
“I have been roaming around Baneshwar market for three days. Dealers say there is no fertilizer. But fertilizer is available only if you secretly pay more money at the market’s retail shops,” farmer Abdur Rahim said.
Another farmer, Rafiqul Islam, said he had queued since 6am only to be told four hours later that stocks had run out.
The protesters alleged that an artificial shortage was being created despite government allocations and demanded supplies of urea, TSP and DAP at fixed prices.
Puthia Upazila Nirbahi Officer Liaquat Salman assured farmers that action would be taken against unscrupulous dealers and fertiliser would be made available at the government-set price.
Dealer Osman Ali rejected allegations of a shortage or manipulation, saying he still had 51 tons of urea in stock, although stocks of some non-urea fertilisers had declined.
The protests in separate districts point to a problem extending beyond headline stock figures.
While authorities repeatedly insist that Bangladesh has adequate fertiliser, farmers on the ground say getting it when needed, and at the government-set price, is becoming increasingly difficult.
With the Aman season under way, the emerging challenge is therefore not simply whether fertiliser exists in warehouses, but whether it is reaching farmers on time, in sufficient quantities and at the price set by the government.

item.title: Beyond the banana raft: Asadul’s story and the road to better education in chars
item.description:
During the monsoon period, going to school was never just a simple walk for Asadul.
The books in his schoolbag often became wet. The muddy path between home and school turned slippery and treacherous. A deep canal stood between his home and the classroom, and when rain came, it swelled into a strong current.
Sometimes he waded through waist-deep water. On other days, he crossed on a raft made of banana trees.
Yet he kept going.
For a boy growing up in the remote char village of Nowshala in Kurigram's Chilmari upazila, school represented something much greater than a classroom. It was a pathway to a different life.
From an early age, Asadul dreamed of becoming a doctor -- a dream that appeared almost impossible in a place where even reaching school became a daily struggle.
Today, that boy is a student at Rangpur Medical College.
His journey is extraordinary, and it also speaks to a much larger reality in Bangladesh.
Over the past decades, the country has made significant progress in bringing children into school. About 97% of primary school-aged children were enrolled in school, while the dropout rate declined significantly from 40% in 2010 to 13% in 2023.
But, for those living in remote and climate-vulnerable areas, the harder challenge is often staying in school, completing secondary education, and finding a pathway to higher education.
Bangladesh has made steady progress in expanding access to education, but significant gaps remain in remote char areas.
The Bangladesh Education Sector Analysis 2026 highlights persistent “last mile” challenges, high dropout rates, and continuing disparities affecting children from low-income households, remote and vulnerable areas, and other marginalized groups.
Asadul's life offers a human face to those statistics.
When he was growing up, there was no school in the vicinity of Nowshala, surrounded by the Brahmaputra River. For the communities, education remained beyond reach.
That began to change in 2006, when Friendship established a primary school in the area. Asadul enrolled in 2008.
He was still young, but he had already seen the harshness of char life.
River erosion repeatedly threatened his family's home and land. Poverty was a constant reality.
Yet while the river could take away land and possessions, it could not take away his determination to study.
"During floods, I sometimes crossed the canal on a banana raft. Often my books and notebooks got wet," Asadul recalls. "But I always felt that if I stopped going to school, my dream would disappear too."
It is difficult to imagine what those words meant to a child who had to negotiate floodwater simply to attend class. But for Asadul, education had already become inseparable from his hope for a better future.
Photo of Asadul at Rangpur Medical College. Photo: Courtesy
After six years of struggle, he completed primary education. Yet the next stage proved even more difficult.
There was still no nearby secondary education opportunity. To continue studying, Asadul had to leave home and depend on others.
He stayed in different households, taught their children, and did household work in exchange for food and accommodation. He also worked in hotels, agricultural farms, and crop-processing centers.
His education was sustained not by comfort, but by sacrifice.
"To continue my studies, I had to move from one house to another. In return, I taught their children and did different kinds of work, he says."
The arrangement was not always kind.
"Sometimes families demanded money for food and accommodation, which I could not afford. I had to leave those places and start again elsewhere. There were days when I worked in other people's homes just to arrange one meal."
Still, he refused to abandon his education.
"I always carried a dream -- to become educated, change my destiny, and bring happiness to my family and society."
His daily routine was grueling: Classes during the day, work in the afternoon and evening, and study late into the night.
Eventually, he completed both secondary and higher secondary education.
Then came the medical admission test.
For Asadul, becoming a doctor had never been simply about choosing a profession. It had become a personal promise -- to himself and to the family whose hardships he had witnessed since childhood.
Guidance and encouragement from mentors helped him gain confidence about higher education and career choices. He began studying 14 to 15 hours a day.
But his first attempt at the medical admission test ended in regret. He missed the opportunity by just two marks.
For many students, such a narrow margin of failure could have ended the dream. For Asadul, it became another reason to try.
The following year, the result he had waited for finally arrived.
In the 2022–23 academic session, Asadul secured admission to Rangpur Medical College.
The distance he had travelled was not merely geographical. It was a journey from a place where a child once had to cross floodwater to reach a primary classroom to a point where that same child could enter one of the country's prominent medical colleges.
"Every night before going to sleep, I feel that I am finally becoming a doctor," he says. "In the future, I want to serve disadvantaged people as a compassionate physician."
His words carry a significance beyond personal achievement.
Bangladesh's education story is often told through enrollment figures and examination results. But behind those numbers are children whose educational journeys are shaped by where they are born, whether their families can afford to keep them in school, whether a road remains passable during the rainy season, and whether they can see a future beyond the next examination.
The challenge is particularly acute in climate-vulnerable communities.
Unicef says children living in disaster-affected parts of Bangladesh are among those most at risk of exclusion from school.
In 2024 alone, climate-related events disrupted the education of 35 million children in Bangladesh, with heatwaves, cyclones, and floods causing repeated school closures and, in some areas, children losing up to eight weeks of learning.
For children in the chars , education must mean more than opening the door of a school. It must mean creating a continuous pathway -- from primary education to secondary school, from secondary school to higher education, and eventually from education to dignified work and meaningful participation in society.
The support of educational initiatives and career guidance can help students from remote communities see possibilities that may otherwise remain invisible.
Asadul’s story is ultimately about what a young person can do when opportunity meets determination. Yet stories like his suggest that something else is changing in Bangladesh’s chars.
As access to education expands, children are beginning to imagine futures as doctors, engineers, teachers, and other professionals.
It reminds us that talent does not belong only to cities, nor does ambition stop at the edge of a river.
This is the larger promise of education in Bangladesh: Not simply getting children into classrooms, but enabling them to stay, learn, progress, and aspire.
Building a better Bangladesh therefore requires more than expanding access. It requires resilient schools and learning opportunities in vulnerable communities, stronger support for children at risk of dropping out, quality learning, pathways from primary to secondary education, career guidance, and opportunities to continue into higher education.
The boy who once crossed floodwaters on a banana raft is now on his way to becoming a doctor.
His story is not only about how far one child has travelled. It is about how far Bangladesh can take its children if education reaches the last mile and the pathway does not end there.
Sometimes, building a better future begins with simply helping a child reach school. The real transformation comes when that child is given the opportunity to keep going.
Ruhul Kuddus is the General Manager of the Education Sector, Friendship.

item.title: Ensuring remittance keeps trending upwards
item.description:
It is encouraging to find that remittance inflows have reportedly increased by 18.6% to $6.05 billion in the current fiscal year, especially at a time when the country continues to navigate economic pressures and needs stronger foreign-exchange earnings.
Remittances have long been one of Bangladesh’s most dependable sources of foreign currency while also providing vital support to millions of families, so the latest growth deserves recognition.
More importantly, this should encourage policy-makers to build on the factors that are helping formal remittance channels become more attractive and accessible.
For a country with a large overseas workforce, there is considerable room to do more: Migrant workers make enormous sacrifices to earn abroad, and ensuring that their hard-earned money can be sent home safely, quickly, and at reasonable cost should be a priority.
Globally, the cost of sending remittances remains significant, with the World Bank reporting an average cost of 6.36% across the corridors it tracks, and Bangladesh must continue working to reduce such costs.
At the same time, the government and financial institutions need to maintain policies that encourage migrants to use official channels. Better exchange rates, simplified procedures, stronger digital services, and greater confidence in the banking system can help sustain the upward trend while reducing reliance on informal methods.
But increasing remittance inflows should not become an excuse for complacency. Bangladesh must ensure that these foreign earnings contribute to broader economic stability and productive investment in long-term economic security rather than merely meeting immediate consumption needs.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive; they demonstrate the continuing contribution of Bangladeshis working overseas and offer some much-needed momentum for the economy.
Now, we must keep the focus on making formal remittance channels even easier, protecting migrant workers’ interests, and creating an environment where every dollar sent home can generate maximum value for families and the country alike.

item.title: Literacy must mean more
item.description:
As we observe International Literacy Day today, it is important to remind ourselves that literacy is not merely the ability to read and write but a fundamental human right and a foundation for accessing wider knowledge, skills, and opportunities.
Yet, it is disheartening that despite decades of progress, at least 739 million young people and adults worldwide still lack basic literacy skills.
For Bangladesh, this remains a particularly relevant concern. The country has made significant strides in expanding access to education, particularly among younger generations: Unesco data put youth literacy at 93.4%, while literacy among those aged 25-64 stands at 76.1%.
These figures show both how far Bangladesh has come and how much work still remains.
More importantly, literacy cannot be treated as a statistic that ends once someone can sign their name or read a sentence. In an increasingly digital society, people must be able to understand information, distinguish fact from misinformation, navigate technology, and also apply what they learn to everyday decisions.
This is especially important in Bangladesh, where access to digital services, financial systems, healthcare information, and government services is rapidly expanding.
The challenge here is twofold: Ensuring that children receive strong foundational literacy and reaching adults who were left behind by the formal education system.
Rural communities, disadvantaged families, older people, and those living in climate-vulnerable areas deserve particular attention.
Encouragingly, Bangladesh already has examples of innovative approaches, such as Sidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha’s solar-powered floating schools, which received Unesco’s Confucius Literacy Prize.
The government must build on such initiatives rather than treating literacy as a campaign-day issue. Better-funded adult education, stronger foundational learning, trained teachers, and accessible digital-literacy programmes are essential.
On this International Literacy Day, Bangladesh should remind itself that literacy is not simply about producing people who can read. It is about empowering citizens to understand, participate, and prosper -- and that must remain the ultimate goal.

item.title: Extortion squeezes Dhaka’s small traders
item.description:
For nearly two decades, Akhtar Mia has run a scrap business on Mazar Road in Gabtoli. Yet keeping his small shop open means paying much more than rent and utility bills.
The 150-square-foot shop costs him around Tk12,000 a month, including other bills. He also pays Tk8,000 every month to three local groups, he said.
Nearby tea-stall owner Amir Hossain pays Tk7,000 in monthly rent and another Tk5,000 to influential local people.
Both names are pseudonyms as the traders fear reprisals.
They said scrap dealers, tea-stall owners, vegetable vendors, cobblers and other small traders routinely have to make such payments to continue doing business.
“This is the rule if you want to do business,” they said.
Their experiences reflect a wider problem across Dhaka, where extortion has become an additional cost for thousands of small traders already struggling with rent, raw materials and household expenses.
Police have identified 1,200 alleged extortionists in Dhaka, underscoring the scale of a problem that traders say persists despite repeated government assurances of a crackdown.
During visits on Sunday and yesterday to Mazar Road, Mohammadpur, Shyamoli, Mirpur and Karwan Bazar, this correspondent found roadside markets and temporary stalls occupying busy roads and public spaces.
Traders said local influential groups regularly collect money from vendors, with the amount varying according to the type and size of business.
A fruit seller on Bosila Road said people monitor who opens a business and how much it earns. Collections continue from evening until late at night, the trader said, with payments starting at around Tk200 a day.
A clothing seller operating from a van on a government road in Shyamoli said he also pays Tk200 a day despite running the business only part-time.
The road from Mohammadpur Krishi Market through Shyamoli to Tajmahal Road is lined with temporary stalls, with trading continuing from noon until late at night.
In Karwan Bazar, traders say extortion has continued despite protests and assurances from the authorities.
Last December, a group of alleged extortionists armed with sticks attacked traders taking part in a human chain against extortion, according to traders.
Although the administration later assured them that action would be taken, traders said the collections continued.
They said they pay Tk200–300 a day, with demands imposed on businesses ranging from scrap dealers to suppliers of raw materials.
Several traders said extortion stopped for a period following the August uprising but resumed after the BNP-led government came to power. They alleged that several groups identifying themselves as local Jubo Dal leaders became involved in collecting money.
The traders said those who refuse to pay or protest risk attacks, threats of murder or the closure of their businesses.
At Shah Ali Mazar Road in Mirpur, an illegal makeshift market stretches from Shah Ali School & College Market Shopping Center to Shah Ali Super Market, occupying roughly two-thirds of the main road.
More than 200 temporary shops selling daily necessities operate there, according to traders.
Vendors said those controlling the market collect Tk50–300 from each shop every day, depending on the type and size of the business.
Most declined to identify the collectors, citing fear of reprisals.
A small businessman alleged that people associated with a political party collect around Tk1 lakh a day from the market.
Ekram Hossain, a resident of Mirpur-4, said such a situation was unacceptable in an independent country.
He also blamed the roadside market for causing persistent traffic congestion and hardship for local residents.
Police have identified 1,200 alleged extortionists operating across Dhaka.
The highest numbers were recorded in Khilkhet, with 112, followed by Kalabagan with 100, Hatirjheel with 77, Mohammadpur with 59 and Badda with 57.
Adabor, Bhatara, Khilgaon, Uttara East and Pallabi are among the other areas with high numbers of identified extortionists.
Police data show that 58% of those on the list are active in these 10 areas.
Police say extortion is particularly prevalent in areas with roadside businesses, transport stands and construction projects, where multiple groups can collect money from the same area.
The police list also includes allegations of law enforcement involvement in 35 extortion incidents, with the highest number reported in the DMP’s Mirpur division.
A senior police official involved in compiling the list said extortionists operate across the capital and often use the names of political or criminal groups to collect money.
Many do not hold formal political positions, the official said, adding that some use the names of political groups to collect money from garment factories, housing developers and suppliers.
The findings point to an extortion system that extends beyond street-level collectors, with alleged links to criminal groups, political influence and weaknesses in enforcement.
AHM Shahadat Hossain, AIG (Media and Public Relations) at Police Headquarters, told Dhaka Tribune on Monday afternoon that police operations were continuing to arrest people on the list.
He said area-based teams were conducting the operations and that more than 150 listed extortionists and their associates had been arrested during special drives.
Many of those on the list are in hiding, he said, adding that operations would continue.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed recently said organized extortionists and drug dealers would be eliminated and warned that law enforcement officials could face action if they failed to prevent crime.
He also said police were identifying extortionists as well as law enforcement personnel allegedly involved with them.
Shahadat urged victims to report extortion to their local police stations or call 999, saying police have been instructed to act on complaints.
Traders, however, say they have yet to see effective action against the networks operating in their areas.
Crime expert and Dhaka University teacher Touhidul Haque said extortion had become a major burden for small businesses and that identifying extortionists or conducting short-term arrest drives would not be enough.
He said authorities must target the broader networks behind extortion, including armed criminals, political figures providing protection, financial beneficiaries and administrative collaborators.
Those facilitating extortion from within law enforcement or the administration should also face legal action, he said.
According to Haque, token arrests will not solve the problem unless the networks behind the collections are dismantled.
He also pointed to weaknesses in the legal process, saying suspects arrested in extortion cases can often secure bail.
The government must close such loopholes and ensure proper investigation and prosecution of extortion cases, he said.
For Dhaka’s small traders, extortion is more than an illegal payment. Every Tk50, Tk200 or Tk300 taken from a roadside vendor comes directly out of a business already operating on narrow margins.
And despite a government pledge to crack down and a police list identifying 1,200 alleged extortionists, traders say extortion remains deeply entrenched across the capital.

item.title: Experts stress research, practice to promote Bengali type design globally
item.description:
Type designers, researchers and typography practitioners have stressed the need for more research and regular practice to further develop Bengali type design and take it to the global stage.
They made the remarks at ‘Lipikola TypeTalk 2026’, organised by Lipikola Type Foundry at the Bishwa Sahitya Kendra building in Banglamotor, Dhaka.
The event focused on the history and contemporary practice of Bengali type design, its aesthetics and technology, research, and its potential in the international arena.
Discussing the key elements of Bengali type design, Dhaka University Graphic Design Professor Maksudur Rahman said the shapes, stylisation and strokes of Bengali letters play a crucial role in developing typefaces.
He said letterforms often change when handwritten or pictorial forms are translated into type, stressing the need to distinguish between calligraphy, typography and other forms of visual marks.
He also noted that type design requires a range of specialised skills, making it difficult for one person to handle every aspect of the process, while such expertise is increasingly in demand internationally.
The discussion also highlighted technological challenges in Bengali typography. New Age Deputy Editor Abu Jar Md Akkas pointed to limitations in Bengali keyboards and Unicode in accessing certain letters and character combinations, saying these gaps can create difficulties for users.
He stressed the need for research into both the history and contemporary practice of type design, as well as greater attention to letter spacing.
Type designer Anisuzzaman Sohel shared a professional memory of receiving praise from late artist Qayyum Chowdhury while working on the Samakal logo.
Organisers said Bengali lettering is an important visual element of the language and culture, but regular and institutional discussions on Bengali type design and typography remain limited.
Type designer and researcher Jacob Thomas, artist and type designer Shahinur Rahman, Avro developer Tanbin Islam Siam and Ekushey Project developer Ami Azad also attended the event.
Established in 2024, Lipikola Type Foundry works on Bengali and multilingual typefaces, research, publications, typography and type culture. Its TypeTalk event was first organised in 2025.

item.title: Democratic United Front demands judicial probe into Rangpur killings
item.description:
A left-leaning political alliance staged a protest in Rangpur on Monday demanding a judicial inquiry into the killing of four members of a family, including a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, and the arrest of those responsible.
The Democratic United Front organised a procession, human chain and rally in the city, alleging that contradictory statements from police had raised questions about the investigation and eroded public confidence in the authorities.
The procession started near the Rangpur Press Club and passed through several major roads before protesters formed a human chain and held a rally in Kachari Bazar, outside the office of the Deputy Commissioner.
Abdul Quddus, Rangpur district coordinator of the Democratic United Front and district convener of the Socialist Party of Bangladesh (SPB), presided over the rally. Kafi Sarker, general secretary of the Rangpur district committee of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), moderated the event.
Speakers included Abdullah Kafi Ratan, general secretary of the CPB and central coordinator of the Democratic United Front, Nazmul Haque Pradhan, general secretary of Bangladesh Jasad, Bazlur Rashid Firoz, general secretary of SPB and coordinator of the Anti-Imperialist Alliance Sima Dutta of SPB (Marxist), Iqbal Kabir Jahid, general secretary of the Revolutionary Communist League of Bangladesh and Marxist leader Anwar Hossain Bablu.
Ganapati Chakraborty, a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, and three members of his family were found killed at their home in Machuapara in Rangpur city.
Police have arrested two suspects, identified by the protesters as Mugdha and Siddhartha Das, in connection with the case. The protesters said police had claimed that the two suspects killed the victims by strangulation after being prevented from using yaba.
The protesters questioned that account, saying drug tests reportedly found no evidence of drug use among the arrested suspects. They also alleged that investigators had not adequately examined possible motives behind the killings.
“The police investigation has lost its credibility among the people,” the speakers said, calling for the case to be investigated under the supervision of a judicial inquiry committee.
They also demanded that the actual perpetrators be identified and arrested and that all possible motives behind the killings be investigated.
The speakers expressed concern over the growing availability of illegal drugs in Rangpur, alleging that drug hotspots and those involved in drug distribution could not be unknown to law-enforcement agencies. They urged the authorities to identify drug suppliers and their alleged patrons and take effective legal action.
They said rising incidents of murder, rape, extortion, robbery and drug-related crime were making people's lives increasingly insecure in Rangpur and elsewhere in Bangladesh.
The protesters warned that failure to ensure a credible investigation and bring the actual killers to justice would lead to stronger protests in Rangpur and across the country.

item.title: Modern cold storage facility nears completion in Bandarban
item.description:
A modern cold storage facility is nearing completion in Bandarban town, offering a much-needed solution to the annual loss of seasonal fruits and vegetables caused by inadequate storage facilities.
The facility, the first of its kind in the district headquarters, is being constructed by the Bandarban unit of the Chattogram Hill Tracts Development Board (CHTDB) at a cost of Tk 1.85 crore and 56 lakh.
Located in the bus station area of Bandarban town, the cold storage will have a capacity to preserve 50 metric tonnes of fruits and other agricultural produce. Construction of the building has largely been completed, while a generator, electrical connections, cooling equipment and other necessary facilities have been installed.
Officials involved in the project said around 95 percent of the work has already been completed and the facility is expected to become operational soon.
Every year, farmers in Bandarban suffer significant financial losses as large quantities of seasonal fruits and vegetables deteriorate because of the lack of proper storage facilities. The new cold storage is expected to reduce post-harvest losses and allow farmers to store their produce until market conditions become more favourable.
Farmers hope the facility will enable them to avoid distress sales during peak harvesting seasons and secure fair prices for their produce.
Abdus Sattar, a farmer from Bandarban Sadar, said the facility would be a major benefit for local growers.
“Although it has taken a long time, we are happy that a cold storage facility is finally being built. Once it becomes operational, we will be able to preserve our agricultural produce and get better prices,” he said.
Lal Piyan Bom, a mango grower from Bandarban Sadar, said the district produces large quantities of Rangwai mangoes and other fruits.
“Bandarban has considerable potential for fruit cultivation. If we have proper storage facilities, we can preserve the fruits and sell them later at better prices,” he said.
According to project sources, construction began in 2023 and is scheduled for completion in 2026.
Abu Bin Mohammad Yasir Arafat, executive engineer of the Bandarban unit of the Chattogram Hill Tracts Development Board, said the project was progressing as planned.
“About 95 percent of the work has already been completed. Once the cold storage becomes operational, farmers will be able to preserve their fruits and other produce for longer periods and earn more from their sales,” he said.

item.title: Power outage disrupts services at Barisal hospital
item.description:
Frequent power outages are causing patients to suffer at Barisal General Hospital and Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital (SBMCH), disrupting treatment and making it difficult to keep operating theatres and critical care units running.
Patients at the hospital face three to four hours of load shedding a day, according to hospital authorities and patients’ relatives.
The department operates from a five-storey building where about 400 patients are admitted on average each day, accompanied by more than 500 relatives, hospital officials said.
When electricity fails, ceiling fans stop working and the crowded wards quickly become difficult to tolerate, particularly for patients suffering from breathing difficulties and other serious illnesses.
“Because of the large number of patients and relatives, it is already very hot inside,” said Abdul Qayum, who has been staying at the hospital with his daughter for seven days. “When the power goes out repeatedly, it feels like we are being boiled.”
Qayum said he bought a rechargeable fan and brought two hand fans to keep his daughter comfortable.
Hospital Director Brigadier General A.K.M. Mashiul Munir said the Medicine Department is served by a single electricity line, unlike the main hospital building, which has two lines and experiences little load-shedding.
“We have requested the Public Works Department to supply 100 litres of fuel every day,” Munir said. But the department has told hospital authorities that there is no government allocation for generator fuel.
The hospital has repeatedly appealed to the ministry for funding, he said.
“The generator is ready, and if we receive fuel, we will be able to provide backup power and reduce the patients’ suffering,” Munir said.
He could not say when the fuel would be available.
Md Faisal Alam, executive engineer at the Barisal Public Works Department, confirmed that the ministry does not currently allocate funds for fuel to operate the hospital generator.
“We have applied for an allocation. Once the allocation is received, fuel will be supplied through a contractor,” Alam said.
He also could not provide a timeframe for the funding.
Power outages are a particular concern in the hospital’s intensive care unit, where staff must closely monitor critically ill patients whenever electricity fails.
“We become worried about the patients when the power goes out,” a nurse working in the ICU said. “As soon as load-shedding begins, we have to remain extra vigilant.”
Relatives often help by arranging rechargeable fans and other necessities during outages, nurses said.
Patients and their families also face practical difficulties beyond the heat. Rahima Begum, who is staying with her husband on the fifth floor, said power cuts disable the hospital’s lift, forcing her to use the stairs whenever she needs to collect food or medicine.
“We came here to make my husband better, but now we are becoming sick ourselves,” she said.
The Barisal electricity grid is supplying only 50 to 55 megawatts against demand of around 85 to 90 megawatts, according to officials at the grid control room.
Officials said the hospital’s main building is protected from regular load-shedding because it has two electricity connections. The Medicine Department building, with only one connection, is subjected to several hours of outages.
The shortage has exposed vulnerabilities in a hospital that serves hundreds of patients each day. Without fuel for its backup generator, a critical department is left without electricity for hours at a time.
For patients struggling with illness in extreme heat, the simplest of cooling devices have become essential: rechargeable fans and hand fans.

item.title: DMCH doctor assault: Two accused placed on 3-day remand
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Monday placed two youths on three-day remand each in a case filed over allegedly assaulting, threatening and demanding extortion from Dhaka Medical College Hospital Professor Dr Md Asadur Rahman.
The accused are Sabbir Hossain, 18, and Fahim Israk Labib, 20.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam passed the order after a hearing in the afternoon. Rokonuzzaman, inspector of the prosecution department, confirmed the matter.
Earlier, Paltan Model Police Station Sub-Inspector Md Atikuzzaman, also the case’s investigating officer, produced the accused before the court and sought 10 days’ remand for each.
According to the remand plea, the accused are active members of an extortion gang operating at various locations in Dhaka and were directly or indirectly involved in the incident. Police said their custodial interrogation was necessary for a proper and impartial investigation.
According to the case statement, Dr Asadur was leaving his chamber at Popular Diagnostic Centre in the capital’s Shantinagar area around 10:00pm on August 17 when he boarded a CNG-run auto-rickshaw.
Shortly after the vehicle started moving, four people intercepted it and demanded that the door be opened. Although the driver was initially told not to open it, he eventually did so.
The assailants then repeatedly beat the doctor, leaving him injured on the head, above both eyes and on various parts of his body.
Hearing his cries, people nearby rushed to the scene and detained one of the suspects, identified as Jibon, while the others fled.
Police from Paltan Model Police Station rescued the doctor and took him to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
Dr Asadur filed the case with Paltan Police Station on August 18.
